questions.q: A gaming company wants a Redis-compatible store for player sessions and leaderboards. It will be the only database, and acknowledged writes must never be lost on failover. Which service fits?

options.t: Amazon ElastiCache for Redis OSS
options.why: Wrong: it is a cache; replication is asynchronous, so recent writes can be lost on failover.

options.t: Amazon MemoryDB
options.why: Right: it keeps data in a Multi-AZ transaction log, so it is a durable primary database with the Redis API.

options.t: Amazon DAX
options.why: Wrong: it only caches DynamoDB and is not a general Redis-compatible database.

options.t: Amazon DocumentDB
options.why: Wrong: it is a document database, not an in-memory store with Redis data structures such as sorted sets.

questions.explain: Redis API + durability + primary database = MemoryDB.
questions.remember: Durable, Redis-compatible, source of truth, no data loss → MemoryDB. Cache in front of another database → ElastiCache.
variants: Cache in front of RDS to speed up reads → ElastiCache (cheaper, no durable log).
Cache only for DynamoDB → DAX.
Serverless, huge, cheap key-value storage → DynamoDB.

questions.q: An application stores 30 TB in MemoryDB, but only about 15% of the data is read regularly. The team wants to cut cost without changing client code. What should they do?

options.t: Move to db.r6gd nodes with data tiering
options.why: Right: cold values move to local SSD by LRU, keys stay in memory, and no client change is needed.

options.t: Move to db.t4g.medium nodes
options.why: Wrong: burstable nodes are for dev/test and are not suited to production.

options.t: Add more replicas to each shard
options.why: Wrong: replicas add read capacity but each costs a full node, so cost rises.

options.t: Put an ElastiCache cluster in front of MemoryDB
options.why: Wrong: it adds a service and cost and does not remove the memory cost of cold data.

questions.explain: Mostly cold data → data tiering on r6gd.
questions.remember: Data tiering fits when about 20% or less of the data is hot; cold values go to SSD, keys always stay in memory.
variants: Data tiering cluster later needs to become r7g → not possible, you cannot scale between tiering and non-tiering node families.
Keys are larger than values → tiering saves little, since keys stay in memory.
Whole dataset is hot → use normal memory-optimized nodes (r7g).

questions.q: A team wants lowest-latency semantic search for a RAG app and already stores key/value data in MemoryDB. The vectors need to scale across many shards. What is the best advice?

options.t: Enable vector search on the existing cluster and add shards
options.why: Wrong: search cannot be enabled on an existing cluster and it is limited to a single shard.

options.t: Use MemoryDB vector search and scale with shards
options.why: Wrong: vector search does not scale horizontally; only vertical scaling and replicas.

options.t: Use OpenSearch or Aurora PostgreSQL pgvector for vectors that exceed one shard
options.why: Right: MemoryDB vector search is fast but memory-bound and single-shard, so large vector sets need another store.

options.t: Use ElastiCache with the t4g node type
options.why: Wrong: it does not solve the scale requirement, and t4g is not for production.

questions.explain: Vectors beyond one shard → OpenSearch or Aurora pgvector.
questions.remember: MemoryDB vector search = fastest, but single shard and enabled at cluster creation. Large scale → OpenSearch or pgvector.
variants: Moderate dataset, lowest latency, key/value access too → MemoryDB vector search.
Add search to an existing cluster → restore a snapshot into a new search-enabled cluster.
Relational data plus HNSW vectors → Aurora PostgreSQL pgvector.

questions.q: A MemoryDB shard has one node and no replica. The primary node fails. What happens?

options.t: A replica is promoted within seconds with no interruption
options.why: Wrong: there is no replica to promote.

options.t: Writes stop until a new primary is built and synced from the transaction log
options.why: Right: with no replica, nothing can be promoted; the log keeps data safe but the new primary must be rebuilt first.

options.t: All acknowledged writes are lost
options.why: Wrong: the transaction log keeps all acknowledged writes, so nothing is lost.

options.t: The cluster switches to another Region automatically
options.why: Wrong: Multi-Region is a separate active-active feature and is not automatic failover.

questions.explain: Single-node shard: no data loss, but writes stop until rebuild.
questions.remember: Always keep at least 1 replica per shard; promoting a replica is faster than building a new primary.
variants: Shard has one replica in another AZ → consistent replica promoted in typically a few seconds.
Whole cluster fails → nodes rebuild from the log, still no data loss.
App wants to test failover → FailoverShard, max 5 times per 24 hours.

questions.q: An application must read its own writes immediately after saving a session. Reads currently go to replicas and sometimes return old data. What should the team change?

options.t: Read from the primary node
options.why: Right: the primary is strongly consistent, including across failover.

options.t: Add more replicas
options.why: Wrong: replicas are eventually consistent, so more of them does not fix staleness.

options.t: Enable data tiering
options.why: Wrong: tiering moves cold values to SSD and does not change consistency.

options.t: Switch to a larger node type
options.why: Wrong: size does not change replica consistency.

questions.remember: Primary = strongly consistent; replicas (READONLY) = eventually consistent but sequentially ordered. Stale reads acceptable → replicas for more read throughput.
variants: Need more read throughput and stale data is OK → read from replicas.
Replica lag visible in CloudWatch → ReplicationLag metric.
Need more write throughput → add shards, not replicas.

questions.q: A security team wants applications to connect to MemoryDB without stored passwords. The cluster runs Valkey 7.2. Which setup meets this?

options.t: Use the open-access ACL
options.why: Wrong: it gives full access to anyone and has no authentication; not for production.

options.t: Create a user with IAM authentication mode and allow memorydb:connect on the cluster and user ARNs
options.why: Right: the client sends a short-lived SigV4 token as the password, so no password is stored.

options.t: Use a security group rule only
options.why: Wrong: it controls network reach only, not user authorization.

options.t: Store the password in the cluster name
options.why: Wrong: cluster names appear in public Certificate Transparency logs.

questions.remember: IAM auth: memorydb:connect on cluster and user ARN; token valid 15 minutes; connection dropped after 12 hours unless re-authenticated; not inside MULTI/EXEC.
variants: Team may only read keys under app:: → ACL user with `on ~app::* -@all +@read`.
Engine below 7.0 → IAM authentication is not available; use ACL passwords.
Cluster without TLS → must use the open-access ACL.

questions.q: A global app needs local reads and writes in several Regions. Two Regions increment the same counter at the same time. What is the result?

options.t: Increments from both Regions are added together
options.why: Wrong: counters use full-value replication, so they do not add up.

options.t: Last writer wins, so one increment can be lost
options.why: Right: Multi-Region uses CRDTs with Last Writer Wins; counters replicate the full value.

options.t: The write that arrived first is kept
options.why: Wrong: conflicts are resolved by last writer, not first.

options.t: Both writes are rejected
options.why: Wrong: active-active accepts writes in each Region; conflicts are resolved afterwards.

questions.explain: MemoryDB Multi-Region is active-active with LWW; counters do not merge.
questions.remember: Strings resolve at key level; hashes, sets and sorted sets at element level; counters last writer wins. Replication is asynchronous, usually under a second.
variants: Two Regions add different hash fields → both survive (element-level resolution).
Need only a DR copy in another Region → copy a snapshot to that Region.
Region is cut off → pending writes replicate when it returns.

questions.q: A team enables a customer managed KMS key for a MemoryDB cluster. Later an administrator disables the key by mistake. What is the impact?

options.t: Nothing; MemoryDB uses its own copy of the key
options.why: Wrong: the cluster depends on the key and its grant.

options.t: The cluster becomes irrecoverable and cannot be modified or recovered after hardware failure
options.why: Right: disabling or deleting the key, or revoking the grant, breaks the cluster.

options.t: Encryption at rest turns off automatically
options.why: Wrong: encryption at rest is always on and cannot be turned off.

options.t: Only the snapshots in S3 become unreadable
options.why: Wrong: the live cluster is also affected, not just snapshots.

questions.explain: Disabled or deleted KMS key → cluster irrecoverable.
questions.remember: Encryption at rest is always on (service-managed key by default). Do not delete, disable or revoke the grant; automatic rotation is fine.
variants: Key scheduled for deletion by mistake → cancel the deletion immediately.
Want a manual key swap → not supported; use automatic rotation.
Exporting a snapshot to S3 → customer managed KMS keys cannot be used for the export itself.
